newsitem.title: UK: FORECAST - UK bosses sanguine over minimum wage.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - UK bosses sanguine over minimum wage.

text.p: Directors of Britain's leading companies believe the European Union (EU) social chapter would be detrimental to business, but a minimum wage would have a negligible impact, a Reuters survey showed on Monday.

In a study of FTSE-100 companies carried out between March 25 and April 1, more than half of the 20 finance and managing directors who responded said they expected a Labour government to take Britain into the European Monetary Union at some stage.

All 20 respondents, none of whom wished to be named, expected Tony Blair's Labour party to topple the ruling Conservatives at the May 1 election. A clear majority of 17 said they would rather place the fortunes of their businesses in Conservative hands.

Opposition Labour, streets ahead in public opinion polls, is poised to introduce a series of measures which critics say could be harmful to British firms. These include acceptance of European workplace rules and the introduction of a minimum wage.
Like the Conservatives, Labour has promised a referendum on entry to the single currency club, but Labour is widely viewed as the more pro-European party.

More than half of the survey's respondents said Labour would make a quick decision on a delayed entry to European economic and monetary union (EMU), while nine thought a decision would be left to a later date.
Only one respondent said a Labour government would decide quickly to take Britain into a single currency from its planned start date in January 1999.
The European Union's social chapter did not go down well with half of the top businesses who responded, the survey showed.

Ten said the chapter, which provides a framework for introducing minimum workplace standards across Europe, would have a fairly negative or a very negative impact on business. The remainder said it would not affect them.

"The overwhelming majority of our members do not want the social chapter. They regard it as burdensome," said Ruth Lea, head of the policy unit at the Institute of Directors. "Clearly most businesses don't want extra employment regulation."
The chapter had been criticised for introducing inflexibility into labour markets at a time when governments were struggling to boost employment.
In its election manifesto announced last Thursday, the Labour party said it would introduce a "sensibly set" minimum wage.
"There must be minimum standards for the individual at work, including a minimum wage within a flexible labour market," the manifesto said.
The TUC favours a minimum wage of 4.26 pounds ($7) an hour, but Labour is expected to plump for a lower level.

An average from nine respondents in the survey showed that businesses expect a level of around four pounds sterling, but would prefer a lower rate. Seven directors gave numbers ranging from zero to four pounds for their preferred level.
Fourteen respondents said a minimum wage would not have a significant impact on business. The other six said it would have a fairly negative effect.

But Lea of the Institute of Directors said a firm's view of a minimum wage would depend on what industry it was in. Also FTSE-100 companies were unlikely to be severely hit as they probably already pay staff above the suggested minimum.
